svg.aria-label: Diagram: publishing a service with Private Service Connect in Google Cloud, the producer side of the previous post; a service attachment points at exactly one target service although several attachments may share one target, and must be created in the same region as that service's load balancer; publishing happens with either automatic approval or explicit approval; access is governed by a consumer accept list and a consumer reject list whose entries must all be of the same type, chosen from project, VPC network, or Private Service Connect endpoint, with folders unsupported and a value appearing on both lists resulting in rejection, and endpoint-level approval achieved by publishing with explicit approval while leaving the lists empty; the dedicated Private Service Connect subnet must be in the same region as the load balancer, may live in a Shared VPC host project, cannot be converted from a regular subnet, cannot be reused across service attachments, and must match the forwarding rule's IP stack with only one address family used on a dual-stack subnet; two numeric knobs, a per-project propagated connection limit defaulting to 250 and NAT IP addresses per accepted endpoint which may be 1 or 2 with 2 raising the ceiling on simultaneous IPv4 connections; PROXY protocol as the only way to see consumer connection information, requiring support from both the target service type and the backend web server; and the domain name field, which needs ownership verified through Google Search Console and may be a subdomain of the verified domain
svg.title: Publishing a service: one attachment, two lists, and two numbers that decide capacity
svg.text: #93 consumed a service. This is the side that decides who may.
The accept list the consumer could not see is the producer’s main instrument — and it has rules.
The service attachment
• Points at a TARGET SERVICE: a supported load balancer, or a Secure Web Proxy instance
• ONE target service per attachment — but MANY attachments may share one target
• Must be in the SAME REGION as that service’s load balancer
AUTOMATIC approval
Any consumer you allow connects
without you approving each one.
EXPLICIT approval
You approve consumers before they
can connect. Also the endpoint-level path.
The two lists, and the four rules that catch people
Every attachment has a CONSUMER ACCEPT LIST and a CONSUMER REJECT LIST. Entries may be a
PROJECT, a VPC NETWORK, or a PRIVATE SERVICE CONNECT ENDPOINT.
1. Every entry must be the SAME TYPE. You cannot mix projects and networks on one attachment.
2. FOLDERS ARE NOT SUPPORTED. No inheriting access down an org tree.
3. On BOTH lists → REJECTED. Reject wins; there is no precedence to tune.
4. To approve INDIVIDUAL endpoints: explicit approval, and leave both lists EMPTY.
The Private Service Connect subnet — the NAT subnet the consumer saw named
• DEDICATED subnets, in the same region as the load balancer
• May live in a SHARED VPC HOST PROJECT
• You CANNOT convert a regular subnet into one. Create it as such or not at all.
• One subnet CANNOT be used in more than one service attachment.
• IP stack must match the forwarding rule: IPv4 rule → IPv4-only or dual-stack; IPv6 rule →
IPv6-only or dual-stack with an internal IPv6 range. On dual-stack, ONE family is used, not both.
Propagated connection limit
Default: 250, PER CONSUMER PROJECT
On automatic approval it applies to each
consumer project that connects.
A per-tenant ceiling, not a service total.
NAT IPs per endpoint
Options: 1 or 2. Default: 1
Setting it to 2 can raise the maximum
simultaneous IPv4 connections an
individual endpoint can establish.
A factor of 2, chosen at publish time.
Two optional fields worth deciding deliberately
PROXY PROTOCOL is the ONLY way to see consumer connection information — #93 noted your
source addresses are translated away. Needs support from the target type AND your web server.
DOMAIN NAME: a DNS name with a TRAILING DOT, recommended REGION.p.DOMAIN. Ownership is
verified through Google Search Console, and a SUBDOMAIN of the verified domain is allowed.
And the constraint that shapes who can consume at all: the IP VERSION of your target service, IPv4 or
IPv6, affects which consumers can connect to your published service.
